atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to aging or heart disease; fatigue, confusion and worsening heart failure can dominate without obvious pallor.
Folate requirements rise sharply in pregnancy; anemia may be detected on routine labs before symptoms, and severe deficiency is linked to neural tube defects in the fetus.
Infants and children may present with poor feeding, irritability, failure to thrive and developmental delay rather than exertional symptoms.
Chronic liver disease and alcohol use often coexist, so the picture may be mixed with other deficiencies and liver-related abnormalities.

labs.caveat: Anemia is macrocytic; hemoglobin falls gradually so symptoms may lag the degree of anemia.
Macrocytosis may be masked by coexisting iron deficiency or thalassemia, which lower the MCV.
Anisocytosis with a high RDW is typical of megaloblastic anemia.
Low or inappropriately normal reticulocyte count confirms a hypoproliferative anemia.
Mild thrombocytopenia can occur with megaloblastic marrow; marked thrombocytopenia suggests another cause.
Leukopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils supports megaloblastic anemia.
Serum folate reflects recent intake and can be falsely low or normal; red cell folate is more stable but less available.
Must be checked to exclude B12 deficiency, which causes identical macrocytic anemia and can be worsened by folate replacement alone.
Elevated from ineffective erythropoiesis and intramedullary hemolysis.
Mild indirect hyperbilirubinemia from ineffective erythropoiesis.
Iron deficiency can coexist and lower the MCV; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may be falsely normal in inflammation.
Hypothyroidism is a common cause of macrocytic anemia and should be excluded.

differential.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia
differential.why_considered: Identical macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia with fatigue, pallor and glossitis; the two are the classic paired look-alikes.
differential.trigger: Macrocytosis with any numbness, tingling, unsteady gait, memory trouble, or a vegetarian diet, pernicious anemia history, or gastric/bariatric surgery

history: Strict vegan diet or long-term metformin or proton pump inhibitor use
Prior gastric or ileal surgery, or known pernicious anemia
exam: Reduced vibration sense or joint position sense
Positive Romberg sign or unsteady gait
Normal neurologic exam does not exclude it
labs: Low serum B12
Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
Elevated intrinsic factor or parietal cell antibodies
Folate level normal

differential.name: Iron deficiency anemia
differential.why_considered: The most common anemia worldwide; causes fatigue, pallor and exertional dyspnea, and can coexist with folate deficiency.

history: Heavy menstrual bleeding or known gastrointestinal blood loss
No alcohol use or poor diet history
Slow chronic blood loss rather than dietary deficiency
exam: No glossitis or a mild one
labs: Low MCV (microcytic) rather than high
Low ferritin and low serum iron with high TIBC
Normal folate and B12
High RDW

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Common reversible cause of macrocytic anemia with fatigue, cold intolerance and cognitive slowing.

history: Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin
exam: Dry coarse skin, delayed relaxation of reflexes, goiter
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
Normal folate and B12
Mild normocytic or macrocytic anemia

differential.name: Alcohol-related macrocytosis and liver disease
differential.why_considered: Heavy alcohol use is a leading cause of both folate deficiency and macrocytosis, and the two frequently overlap.

labs: Macrocytosis may be present even with normal folate
Elevated AST greater than ALT, elevated GGT
Thrombocytopenia and low albumin from liver disease
Folate may be low or normal
imaging: Hepatic steatosis or cirrhosis on ultrasound

differential.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Marrow failure with macrocytic anemia, cytopenias and fatigue, especially in older adults.
differential.trigger: Macrocytic anemia with leukopenia or thrombocytopenia that does not respond to folate replacement, or blasts or dysplastic cells on smear

history: No dietary or alcohol risk factors
labs: Pancytopenia or bicytopenia
Normal folate and B12
Blasts or dysplastic neutrophils on peripheral smear
Bone marrow biopsy shows dysplasia or increased blasts

differential.name: Reticulocytosis from hemolysis or blood loss
differential.why_considered: Anemia with elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin can mimic megaloblastic anemia, and high cell turnover can deplete folate.

history: Jaundice, dark urine, family history of anemia
Sudden onset after a drug or infection
labs: High reticulocyte count rather than low
Positive direct antiglobulin test or abnormal hemoglobin studies
Normal or high folate

differential.name: Medication-induced macrocytosis
differential.why_considered: Methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin, sulfasalazine and hydroxyurea can cause macrocytic anemia and interfere with folate metabolism.

history: Temporal relationship to starting a culprit medication
Underlying condition being treated (rheumatoid arthritis, seizure disorder, inflammatory bowel disease)
labs: Macrocytosis with normal or low folate depending on the drug
Improvement after stopping or adjusting the medication
Normal B12

severity.mild: Hemoglobin 10.0-11.9 g/dL; fatigue and pallor with exertion only; no tachycardia at rest; no neurologic or cardiac findings
severity.moderate: Hemoglobin 8.0-10.0 g/dL; fatigue and exertional dyspnea; mild tachycardia; glossitis may be present; comfortable at rest
severity.severe: Hemoglobin 6.5-8.0 g/dL; dyspnea on minimal exertion, tachycardia, flow murmur, possible high-output heart failure; may need transfusion
severity.critical: Hemoglobin below 6.5 g/dL or symptomatic anemia with hemodynamic instability, confusion, chest pain or heart failure; requires urgent transfusion and inpatient care

red_flags.finding: Confusion, lethargy or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Severe anemia with cerebral hypoperfusion; urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Numbness, paresthesias, unsteady gait or memory loss
red_flags.meaning: Suggests B12 deficiency rather than isolated folate deficiency; giving folate alone can worsen neurologic injury

red_flags.finding: Pancytopenia or blasts on the peripheral smear
red_flags.meaning: Suggests marrow failure or myelodysplastic syndrome rather than a simple vitamin deficiency

special_populations.differences: Folate requirements rise sharply; deficiency is linked to neural tube defects and preterm birth. Supplementation is recommended before conception and through early pregnancy, and anemia may be found on routine labs before symptoms.

Symptoms may be attributed to aging or heart disease; fatigue, confusion and worsening heart failure can dominate without obvious pallor. Poor diet, alcohol use and polypharmacy are common contributors.

Infants and children may present with poor feeding, irritability, failure to thrive and developmental delay rather than exertional symptoms; consider inborn errors of folate metabolism in severe early cases.
Chronic liver disease and alcohol use often coexist, so the picture may be mixed with other deficiencies and liver-related abnormalities; macrocytosis may persist after folate repletion.
Dialysis patients lose folate and may need supplementation; anemia is often multifactorial from erythropoietin deficiency, iron deficiency and folate loss.

key_questions.question: What do you typically eat in a day, and has your diet changed recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor intake of leafy green vegetables, legumes and fortified grains; food insecurity or a restrictive fad diet

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy or daily alcohol use, which both lowers intake and impairs folate absorption and storage

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant, or could you be pregnant? Are you breastfeeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy or lactation, which sharply increase folate requirements

key_questions.question: When did the tiredness start, and how has it changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months with slowly worsening fatigue and exertional dyspnea

key_questions.question: Does your tongue hurt or feel sore, and have you noticed mouth sores?
key_questions.looking_for: Sore, smooth, red tongue or oral ulcers suggesting megaloblastic change

key_questions.question: Any numbness, tingling, unsteady walking, or trouble with memory?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in isolated folate deficiency; present suggests B12 deficiency, which must not be missed

key_questions.question: Have you had stomach or intestinal surgery, or been told you have celiac disease or a malabsorption problem?
key_questions.looking_for: Malabsorption from celiac disease, tropical sprue or bariatric surgery

key_questions.question: Do you take methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, or any seizure medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: A medication that interferes with folate metabolism or absorption

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your stool, black stools, or heavy periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; blood loss points toward iron deficiency or a mixed anemia

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea, weight loss, or a poor appetite?
key_questions.looking_for: Diarrhea and weight loss suggesting malabsorption or poor intake

key_questions.question: Any chest pain, fainting, or shortness of breath at rest?
key_questions.looking_for: Demand ischemia or hemodynamic compromise from severe anemia requiring urgent care

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have anemia or a blood disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of anemia or hemoglobinopathy that would suggest an alternative cause

accepted_names: Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
reasoning_points: Gradual fatigue, pallor and exertional dyspnea with a macrocytic anemia on CBC
Low serum folate with a normal B12 level, since B12 deficiency causes an identical megaloblastic picture
Risk factor identified: poor diet, alcohol use, pregnancy or lactation, malabsorption, or a folate-interfering medication
Low or inappropriately normal reticulocyte count confirming a hypoproliferative anemia
Supporting findings such as elevated LDH, mild indirect hyperbilirubinemia, or hypersegmented neutrophils
No neurologic findings such as paresthesias, impaired vibration or position sense, or unsteady gait
B12 checked before or with folate, because giving folate alone can worsen untreated B12 deficiency
Alternative causes considered and excluded: B12 deficiency, iron deficiency, hypothyroidism, alcohol-related macrocytosis, myelodysplastic syndrome, hemolysis and drug-induced macrocytosis
